A.problem: AI scientist pipelines exhibit hallucinated results, circular confirmations, and subtle integrity failures. Existing responses—generator self-critique and post-hoc verification against already-collected evidence—leave the generator in control of evidence, and falsification has not been implemented as an adversarial selection step between generation and surfacing nor measured against ground-truth hypothesis labels.
A.motivation: Independent evaluations documenting these failures make integrity interventions urgent; an architecture-level selection step could make AI-generated science conservative by default, and a negative result would be equally informative by localizing the bottleneck in raw verifier capability rather than incentive structure.
A.proposed_approach: Before a generated hypothesis is surfaced, it must survive a pre-registered number of independent, hostile falsification attempts, each rewarded only for refutation. Falsifiers select attacks from a curator-maintained challenge pool of simulators, datasets, and literature contrasts, rather than from experiments proposed by the generator. The work also introduces a benchmark of 1,000 truth-labeled hypotheses across physics, chemistry, and biomedicine, including expert-authored plausible falsehoods of the kind found in AI-scientist output.
A.research_plan: On the introduced benchmark, the survival-gating mechanism will be compared with generation-only, self-critique, and confirmation-testing baselines using the known ground-truth labels, measuring precision of surfaced hypotheses and the associated recall cost. Support for the core claim requires higher precision at a measurable recall cost; a negative result would be interpreted as localizing the bottleneck in raw verifier capability rather than incentive structure.

B.problem: End-to-end AI-scientist systems accept hypotheses using machinery epistemically aligned with the generator, amplifying self-bias; static LLM verifiers fail to detect errors, and existing trust scaffolding for agentic discovery gates on artifacts, provenance, or Type-I error control for externally supplied hypotheses rather than training an agent to attack the candidate hypothesis itself.
B.motivation: Trustworthy hypothesis acceptance in automated discovery requires adversarial scrutiny of candidate hypotheses, and the capacity to train agents against in-silico oracles with hidden ground truth now makes such falsification feasible.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed architecture has two adversarial agents: a proposer is rewarded for hypotheses that survive, while a falsifier is deliberately blinded to the proposer's reasoning, data, and provenance. The falsifier is trained by reinforcement learning to design experiments whose measured outcomes contradict the candidate hypothesis; its reward is disconfirmation against an in-silico oracle with hidden ground truth. This reward structure pushes it to probe extrapolation regions where a law that merely fits the proposer's data breaks down.
B.research_plan: The claim is evaluated on rediscovery benchmarks with known but masked mechanisms. The adversarial gate is compared against self-refinement, prompted independent critics, and Popper-style sequential falsification; measured quantities are precision of accepted hypotheses, recall, and oracle queries. Support requires higher precision than the baselines while recall and oracle-query cost remain bounded and measurable; failure is no precision gain or unacceptable cost.

A.problem: Current large-language-model experiment planners for self-driving chemistry laboratories are insensitive to experimental feedback: permuting observed outcomes leaves their behavior unchanged, and they underperform classical Bayesian optimization. They do not commit to causal hypotheses about why a reaction fails, design experiments that discriminate among them, or update beliefs from every outcome.
A.motivation: Self-driving chemistry laboratories increasingly rely on LLM planners, but agents that ignore experimental feedback cannot diagnose failures or allocate experiments effectively. Making this capability testable would let an 'AI scientist' be scored by whether its beliefs change correctly when a reaction fails rather than by proposal quality.
A.proposed_approach: The work introduces an interactive benchmark in which an agent must diagnose one of four hidden reaction-failure causes—oxygen-induced catalyst deactivation, protodeboronation, over-irradiation decomposition, or reagent-batch contamination—from multi-channel observations under an experiment budget. The benchmark includes a placebo outcome-permutation control that directly measures feedback sensitivity. The proposed agent is two-layered: an LLM proposes and interprets structured mechanistic hypotheses, while an explicit Bayesian belief core owns posterior updating, information-gain acquisition, escalation, and stopping.
A.research_plan: The evaluation uses the interactive benchmark to compare LLM-only planners with the proposed agent on hidden-cause diagnosis under an experiment budget, and uses a placebo outcome-permutation control to measure feedback sensitivity (claims 1 and 2). The proposed agent is also compared against hypothesis-free Bayesian optimization at equal budget on diagnosis performance (claim 2). Ablations remove the hypothesis-commitment layer and the probabilistic belief core to test whether either is necessary (claim 3). Support for the central claims consists of LLM-only planners remaining near chance and nearly insensitive under permutation, while the proposed agent diagnoses accurately, exceeds the optimization baseline, degrades under permutation, and loses performance in both ablations. Failure would be indicated if the proposed agent remained accurate under outcome permutation or if removing either component left performance intact.

B.problem: Autonomous research agents are evaluated almost exclusively on deterministic code-execution tasks rather than on the decisions that dominate bench science — which costly, noisy physical experiment to run next and when to stop and report a mechanistic conclusion; in catalysis, the highest-value output of iterative experimentation is often a discriminated mechanism and rate law, not a measured optimum.
B.motivation: This shifts the emerging agentic-science evaluation agenda toward experiment-selection decision quality grounded in physical chemistry, aligning evaluation with the costly, noisy choices that produce mechanistic insight in catalysis.
B.proposed_approach: A reproducible benchmark generates noisy reaction-progress data from a library of oxidation-relevant catalytic mechanisms and treats identification of a hidden mechanistic rate-law model as the unit of scientific output. The hybrid planner uses an LLM to propose and revise an explicit structured set of rival mechanistic hypotheses, while a statistically principled acquisition engine selects each experiment by expected information gain for hypothesis discrimination and decides when to stop.
B.research_plan: (1) The at-least-40% experiment-reduction claim is tested by running the hybrid planner against yield-maximizing Bayesian optimization, pure-LLM planners, and fixed-library discrimination baselines on the benchmark and comparing the number of experiments needed to identify the hidden mechanism; the claim fails if the reduction is below 40%. (2) The feedback-sensitivity claim is tested by a mandatory label-permutation control; failure to show sensitivity to permuted experimental feedback would undermine the claim.

A.problem: Materials science lacks innovative tools sufficient to accelerate knowledge discovery at the pace scientific progress requires.
A.motivation: Accelerating knowledge discovery would support the rapid advancement of scientific progress in materials science.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework organizes a team of LLM agents to collaboratively generate, evaluate, and refine research ideas, and to design and execute experiments.
A.research_plan: Comprehensive experiments compare the proposed framework with state-of-the-art methods on producing novel scientific ideas and accelerating scientific discovery; the abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, or failure conditions.

B.problem: LLM-based approaches to scientific discovery have shown promise in hypothesis generation and experimental design, but they fall short of replicating the collaborative nature of real-world scientific practices.
B.motivation: Scientific progress requires innovative tools to accelerate knowledge discovery, so methods that better emulate collaborative scientific teamwork are needed.
B.proposed_approach: An LLM-based multi-agent system that organizes a team of agents to collaboratively generate, evaluate, and refine research ideas, mimicking the teamwork inherent in scientific research.
B.research_plan: The abstract reports a comparative evaluation of the proposed multi-agent system against state-of-the-art methods on producing novel scientific ideas.

A.problem: Scientific AI systems can generate hypotheses and explanations, but many optimize plausibility more than refutability, leaving hypotheses without systematic adversarial testing or machine-checkable proof.
A.motivation: Making discovery depend on disciplined claim survival rather than fluent claim production could reduce false hypotheses and increase the reliability of machine-generated scientific knowledge.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed architecture coordinates specialized agents that propose hypotheses, build causal models, design adversarial tests, and verify formal claims. These agents operate over a persistent shared memory that records assumptions, counterexamples, interventions, and proof obligations. Failed predictions and invalid proof attempts are treated as learning signals to refine hypotheses rather than being ignored.
A.research_plan: The paper evaluates the framework on simulated discovery tasks using verified discovery rate and false-positive hypothesis retention as evidence for the effectiveness claim. Scaling experiments vary the number of agents and track a discovery quality factor to test the scaling claim. The abstract does not name explicit baselines or failure conditions, though support and failure would turn on the verified discovery and false-positive retention metrics.

B.problem: Current AI-scientist agents and scientific-hypothesis generators are overwhelmingly confirmation-positive: they propose a hypothesis, gather supporting evidence, refine it through LLM self-critique, and treat refuted candidates as dead ends whose content is discarded. When falsification appears, it is a terminal validation gate — Popper-style agents falsify hypotheses that are already on the table, but their verdicts never constrain what the proposer may say next.
B.motivation: Making falsification a first-class search constraint could allow agents to avoid re-proposing refuted ideas and to use anomalies to guide later proposals; existing benchmarks and a new failure-mode benchmark make the comparison measurable.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed architecture has four core parts. For each executed refutation, it stores the smallest set of a hypothesis's commitments that jointly falsify it; it enforces those stored refutations as hard negative constraints on all future proposals; it converts each contradicted prediction into an explanatory obligation that subsequent hypotheses must explain; and it selects experiments adversarially, biasing probes toward disconfirming the current best hypothesis while discriminating among live alternatives. The components are designed to be modular so each can be ablated independently.
B.research_plan: The primary claim is tested at a matched experiment budget across BoxingGym environments, LLM-SRBench discovery tasks, and a new failure-mode benchmark engineered to punish confirmation myopia. The proposed architecture is compared against equal-budget confirmation-driven refinement, surprise-driven open-ended search, and generate-then-falsify pipelines. Support for the claim requires higher accuracy, higher expected information gain per experiment, and a lower rate of re-proposing previously refuted ideas relative to these baselines; failure to show such improvements under matched budgets would count against the claim. Independent ablation of the component that stores and enforces refutations and the component that selects disconfirming experiments isolates their respective contributions.

A.problem: Generating high-quality hypotheses in scientific research is challenging and time-consuming, and current LLM-based approaches show promise but can be further improved in effectiveness.
A.motivation: Automating hypothesis generation could reduce the time and effort required for scientific research; recent advances in LLMs make this tractable, and evolutionary algorithms are well-suited for exploring complex search spaces and optimizing solutions.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed work develops a framework that integrates LLMs with evolutionary algorithms to automate and optimize hypothesis generation. The evolutionary algorithm component is used to explore complex search spaces and optimize candidate solutions, while LLMs support hypothesis generation.
A.research_plan: The framework will be evaluated across various scientific domains to assess performance, efficiency, and innovation. No baselines, metrics, or failure conditions are specified, and no matched controls or ablations are described.

B.problem: Existing LLM-assisted approaches to scientific idea generation exhibit semantic convergence, which limits the diversity and novelty of generated research ideas.
B.motivation: As LLMs show promise in assisting idea generation, overcoming semantic convergence is valuable for broadening the candidate ideas and advancing scientific progress.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework recasts scientific idea generation as an evolutionary search over a population of ideas. It iteratively applies rank-based mutation with differentiated retrieval planning to incorporate external knowledge, and semantic-aware crossover to fuse complementary concepts for conceptual reorganization. A lightweight evaluation signal guides selection, encouraging sustained exploration while mitigating premature convergence.
B.research_plan: The evidence is extensive experiments comparing the proposed framework to state-of-the-art baselines on novelty, diversity, and idea quality under the current automatic evaluation protocol. Claims about enhanced exploration and maintained quality are supported by these comparisons; no explicit failure condition is stated in the abstract.

A.problem: In current autonomous AI scientists, experimental feedback is used to generate and rank hypotheses, but failure diagnosis and hypothesis revision are treated as separate processes, so feedback is not used to explicitly repair failed hypotheses.
A.motivation: Recent agent-debugging work provides explicit error taxonomies that can be adapted to structure failure diagnosis, making it newly tractable to couple diagnosis with automatic hypothesis reformulation.
A.proposed_approach: The framework couples structured failure diagnosis with automatic hypothesis reformulation. It uses explicit error taxonomies adapted from recent agent-debugging work and maps failure patterns—measurement errors, confounding variables, implementation gaps, scoping issues—to targeted hypothesis-repair operations. The revision component is implemented as a module that can be integrated with existing autonomous scientists. A benchmark of 200+ hypothesis-testing tasks across chemistry, biology, and materials science is provided for evaluation.
A.research_plan: The two core claims are evaluated on a benchmark of 200+ hypothesis-testing tasks across chemistry, biology, and materials science, comparing the proposed framework against feedback-only baselines that use experimental outcomes for ranking alone. The metrics are hypothesis quality and experimental convergence time; support requires improvement over those baselines and failure is absence of improvement.

B.problem: AI scientist systems treat experiment failures as terminal events rather than learning opportunities, and no systematic mechanism exists to extract causal insights from failed experiments and use them to reformulate hypotheses.
B.motivation: Recent work has documented failure modes in autonomous research pipelines, making failure traces available for analysis; learning from negative results is a core capability of human researchers and could improve hypothesis quality and experimental efficiency.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed approach is a module for autonomous research pipelines that analyzes why experiments failed, identifies confounding and causal factors in failure traces, and generates revised hypotheses that address the identified failure modes. It is evaluated on a benchmark of hypothesis-driven tasks designed to have high failure rates, comparing systems with and without failure-driven revision. The expected contributions also include a formalized framework for learning from negative results and benchmark resources for failure-driven discovery.
B.research_plan: Evaluation uses a benchmark of hypothesis-driven tasks with high failure rates, comparing systems with failure-driven revision against baselines that ignore failure traces, with hypothesis quality and experimental efficiency as the stated evaluation targets. The abstract does not specify metrics, baselines, or matched controls; implied support requires improvement over the failure-ignoring baselines and failure if no improvement is observed.

A.problem: Closed-loop molecular optimization typically selects experiments by predicted property acquisition rather than maintaining and discriminatively testing competing structural hypotheses about the target's activity mechanism, and existing evaluation does not jointly measure sample efficiency, mechanism recovery, and falsification compliance.
A.motivation: LLM-based agents now make hypothesis-ledger planning feasible, and limited oracle budgets make selective, discriminative experimentation critical; jointly measuring mechanism recovery and falsification compliance could expose what property-accuracy metrics alone hide.
A.proposed_approach: The work releases a benchmark of molecular optimization tasks with planted, hidden ground-truth activity mechanisms (e.g., a specific pharmacophore–target interaction term or a scaffold-gated ADME trade-off) embedded in cheap surrogate oracle models. It also builds a multi-agent LLM system that maintains a versioned ledger of competing structural hypotheses about the target's activity mechanism and whose experiment planner scores each candidate next experiment by expected information gain across the competing hypotheses, not merely by predicted activity.
A.research_plan: Agents are scored on three axes: sample efficiency against an oracle query budget, mechanism recovery (match between the agent's surviving final ledger and the planted mechanism), and falsification compliance (whether retired hypotheses were truly falsified and whether surviving ones are consistent with all observed data). The work benchmarks against black-box Bayesian optimization, GFlowNet-style generators, and ledger-free LLM agents, plus an ablation isolating hypothesis tracking from discriminative experiment selection. Claim (1) is assessed by whether the ledger agents reach activity targets in fewer oracle queries than black-box generators while recovering the planted mechanism; claim (2) is assessed by whether property-accuracy-only metrics conceal the falsification machinery measured by the scored axes.

B.problem: Current AI-driven cell-free protein synthesis pipelines optimize yield but treat the underlying transcription-translation synthesis mechanism as a black box, so the true rate-limiting mechanisms of in vitro protein synthesis remain unidentified.
B.motivation: Recent LLM-agentic hypothesis generation and information-theoretic experiment selection make automated mechanistic discovery feasible, and identifying the true mechanism with calibrated parameters would support rational optimization beyond black-box yield maximization.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is an end-to-end autonomous loop with four components: a curated library of competing kinetic hypotheses for transcription-translation in cell-free lysates; an LLM-agentic hypothesis module that proposes, refines, and enumerates mechanism candidates from literature and prior data; a numeric surrogate engine that simulates each candidate under arbitrary experiment conditions; and an information-theoretic experiment selector that designs batched 96-well discriminator experiments. The selected experiments are validated on the wet bench and scored by an updated Bayesian model-selection posterior, which feeds back into hypothesis refinement.
B.research_plan: To test the core claim, the paper details a benchmark with experimenter-set ground-truth mechanisms on synthetic data and validated standards in real lysates, and compares the loop against LLM-only hypothesis ranking, black-box active learning, and classical D-optimal design. It also runs ablations of the agent components and permuted-label controls to test whether the loop uses feedback. Support would be recovering the ground-truth mechanism with fewer wet-lab cycles and higher discrimination precision than the baselines while producing calibrated mechanistic parameters; failure would be failing to outperform the baselines or showing no loss of performance under permuted labels.

A.problem: Automated structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction remains bottlenecked by crystallographic disorder, partial site occupancies, and solid solutions that violate ideal periodic lattices. Existing generative machine learning approaches predict pristine crystal structures and break down on real-world disordered materials.
A.motivation: Automating structure determination for disordered materials would remove a major bottleneck in materials characterization and extend machine-learning structure prediction to real-world solid solutions and high-pressure phases.
A.proposed_approach: An autonomous AI agent framework couples a disorder-aware generative diffusion prior with automated, physics-guided Rietveld refinement loops. The agent iteratively proposes structural models incorporating fractional site occupancies and atomic displacement parameters, simulates their diffraction patterns, computes residuals against experimental PXRD data, and optimizes parameters using Bayesian optimization.
A.research_plan: Evidence is an empirical evaluation on benchmark disordered solid solutions from the ICSD and newly synthesized high-pressure phases, with existing rigid generative models as baselines; the implied success condition is robust convergence to experimental PXRD data, and failure would be non-convergence or large residuals on disordered cases.

B.problem: While machine learning has automated phase mapping and probabilistic classification, full quantitative structural analysis via Rietveld refinement remains a major bottleneck because automated fitting is fragile, suffering from parameter divergence, false local minima, and inability to handle unmodeled structural disorder or solid solutions without expert intervention.
B.motivation: High-throughput materials discovery relies on powder X-ray diffraction for structural characterization, and removing the expert intervention needed for Rietveld refinement would let automation extend beyond phase mapping to full quantitative analysis.
B.proposed_approach: The framework couples an LLM reasoning engine with programmatic crystallographic backend APIs such as GSAS-II in a multi-agent setup; during iterative Rietveld refinement it parses residual difference plots, diagnoses parameter correlations such as atomic displacement parameters versus site occupancies, and systematically applies crystallographic constraints.
B.research_plan: The intended evidence is an evaluation protocol on experimental inorganic combinatorial libraries and disordered solid solutions, comparing the proposed iterative agentic refinement against traditional heuristic solvers with convergence failures as the failure condition. The protocol assesses whether the framework avoids parameter divergence, false local minima, and failures on unmodeled structural disorder or solid solutions.

A.problem: Existing work splits scientific discovery into separate stages: LLM agents propose explanations but struggle to design informative experiments, while Bayesian experiment-design methods assume a fixed parametric hypothesis class and cannot incorporate hypotheses as they arrive.
A.motivation: A hybrid that lets an LLM generate and revise theories while a Bayesian core schedules experiments would enable autonomous agents to simultaneously test hypotheses and choose measurements, answering calls to separate prior-based reasoning from posterior-updated acquisition.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed architecture has an LLM propose and revise candidate scientific models at discrete revision points. A Bayesian core treats the hypothesis set as a discrete random variable, maintains a posterior over model identity via Bayes factors against acquired data, and selects each experiment by maximizing expected information gain about model identity, estimated with an adapted variational estimator. Each hypothesis carries its own Gaussian process surrogate whose kernel or mean encodes the hypothesis structure, so model identity and next measurement location are answered by the same acquisition function.
A.research_plan: Evidence comes from evaluation on the BoxingGym benchmark environments, measuring experiments-to-discrimination and cumulative expected information gain, and on a new suite of confusable symbolic-dynamics laws, measuring experiments-to-correct-law and final predictive error against GP-ensemble baselines. Claim (1) is tested by comparing expected information gain over model identity against random, uncertainty-sampling, and predictive-error Bayesian optimization under equal experiment budgets; support requires strictly greater realized model-discrimination information. Claim (2) is tested by an outcome-permutation feedback test, with support requiring performance degradation under permuted labels in contrast to LLM-alone design. Claim (3) is tested by comparing final models from LLM revision grounded in numeric posterior-evidence reports against free-form LLM revision; support requires better final models under grounded revision.

B.problem: Autonomous AI scientists can propose equations, run experiments, and draft manuscripts, but none selects the next experiment to discriminate between competing functional forms of the law being discovered.
B.motivation: This matters because resolving which functional form is true is needed for out-of-domain extrapolation and for settling contested laws; current systems only fit fixed data or reduce regression uncertainty for a presumed expression.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed closed-loop system interleaves three components: an LLM-driven symbolic hypothesis generator constrained by physics templates, which maintains a bounded pool of candidate closed-form laws for target observables (transverse vortex-induced-vibration amplitude, cylinder-added damping, or sphere drag coefficient); a Bayesian scoring module that assigns posterior mass over candidate families and parameterizations after each measurement; and an information-gain planner that selects the next experimental setting (flow speed, forcing frequency/amplitude, cylinder phase) to maximize one-step mutual information about which model is true rather than regression error. The agent terminates when the posterior concentrates and outputs the winning interpretable law with a Bayes-factor evidence table. It is validated on the contested sphere-drag problem, comparing logarithmic versus power-series forms of the drag coefficient as a function of Reynolds number, and on vortex/wake-induced vibration transverse-amplitude response through lock-in, benchmarked under the same conditions as the AI Fluid Scientist.
B.research_plan: (1) The discrimination and termination claim is evaluated on the contested sphere-drag problem and on vortex/wake-induced vibration transverse-amplitude response through lock-in, benchmarked under the same conditions as the AI Fluid Scientist; success is measured by number of experiments to reach 95% posterior concentration, parsimony of the winning law, and out-of-domain extrapolation. (2) The agent outputs a Bayes-factor evidence table when the posterior concentrates, serving as evidence for the winning law against alternatives. (3) The first-integration claim is supported by contrasting the system with existing discovery agents, uncertainty-minimizing acquisition methods, and discrimination methods lacking candidate laws or fluid-mechanics benchmarks, rather than by matched experimental baselines. No explicit failure condition beyond the posterior-concentration stopping rule is stated.

A.problem: Topic modeling quality is jointly determined by an under-specified, interacting set of decisions (representation, model family, topic count, regularization, clustering thresholds), but existing systems fit each choice once under hand-tuned defaults and never revise it in light of measured topic quality.
A.motivation: LLM agents make automated iterative revision feasible, and a dedicated benchmark would provide a cheap, scalable proving ground for AI-scientist capabilities that current end-to-end systems cannot isolate.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework has two components: a reproducible benchmark of topic-modeling construction tasks spanning multiple corpora, text granularities, and compute budgets; and an LLM-agent controller that treats model construction as iterative scientific discovery — proposing a pipeline configuration, fitting it, reading a multi-objective diagnostic panel (NPMI coherence, topic diversity, stability, outlier ratio), and revising under an energy budget. The judge component follows Chiang and Lee's LLM-evaluation protocol and is validated against a held-out human panel.
A.research_plan: Claim (1) is tested under an equal fitting-time budget by comparing the agent loop against one-shot BERTopic defaults and a budget-matched exhaustive grid search on the benchmark, with topic quality measured by word-intrusion accuracy and calibrated topic ranking from the judge component, itself validated against a held-out human panel. Failure would be failing to reach higher quality than the baselines, especially on adversarial corpora.

B.problem: Modern neural topic modeling pipelines are static: embedding model, clusterer, topic count, and representation procedure are fixed once, and poor choices surface only as uninformative, duplicate, or outlier-dominated output after the fact; LLM-based topic approaches remain human-steered one-shot systems, and closed-loop research agents have not been applied inside a single data-analysis task where quality signals are directly computable.
B.motivation: Autonomous closed-loop revision could avoid uninformative, duplicate, or outlier-dominated topics without manual after-the-fact inspection, and LLM agents plus directly computable topic-quality signals make such a loop feasible inside a single analysis task.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed self-refining LLM agent makes the entire neural topic-model configuration mutable state—topic count, embedder/clusterer choices, topic-definition prompts, and anchor constraints—and improves it through a closed loop. An internal self-evaluation module computes quantitative quality signals (topic coherence, outlier ratio, inter-topic definition similarity, prevalence distribution), emulating AHAM's metrics but used in-model. A model-selection module proposes candidate states from historical feedback, extrapolating Bayesian topic-number selection into an LLM-driven search, and a reflective synthesis step emits targeted edits such as merge, split, relabel, and constrain. The loop runs autonomously until a convergence criterion terminates unproductive search paths, then halts at a minimal human checkpoint for acceptance or relabeling.
B.research_plan: Evidence is organized around the claims: (1) overall topic-quality alignment is tested against static BERTopic at oracle K, TopicGPT, and ablations of each loop mechanism on 20 Newsgroups, AG News, and an arXiv-domain corpus with gold topic labels, using blind human evaluation as the alignment gold standard; (2) the claim that internal signals predict human judgment is tested by calibrating the computed quality signals against blind human judgments; (3) the contribution of each loop mechanism is isolated through ablations. The loop's convergence criterion defines when unproductive search paths terminate, but the abstract does not state explicit quantitative failure thresholds or matched compute/parameter budgets for the trade-off comparisons.

A.problem: Existing research-idea generators maximize novelty or diversity, and topic-recombination novelty measures are retrospective; no system uses a time-resolved topic network to decide how far to push an idea, and no such measure has been validated on future outcomes.
A.motivation: Connecting these lines could let generators target the regime where topic-combination novelty and feasibility are jointly high, and make novelty scoring a future-validated signal rather than a retrospective one.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed closed-loop pipeline builds a temporal topic network from a time-stamped corpus, scores candidate topic pairs with a bridge potential targeting an intermediate regime of under-exploration, semantic distance, and emergence trend, and feeds that score as an explicit control signal into an LLM ideation agent instructed to hit a target regime rather than maximize novelty. Validation is prospective: scores computed only from papers up to year T are used to predict topic pairs realized in high-impact papers at T+1 through T+3.
A.research_plan: (1) The prediction claim is tested by a strict temporal holdout: the calibrated bridge score, computed only from papers up to T, must predict topic pairs realized in high-impact papers at T+1..T+3 better than distance-only and co-occurrence-only scores; support requires better prediction, failure if not. (2) The steering claim is tested by comparing ideas generated when steering to the calibrated regime against maximal-distance pairing on joint novelty and feasibility; support requires higher joint values. Ablations remove each score term and swap the target for pure novelty maximization, isolating whether calibration rather than novelty itself is responsible.

B.problem: How to identify research gaps from literature-mined topics has no calibrated predictive formulation; current AI-scientist idea generation is assessed by whether the best candidate matches a later or held-out paper, a postdiction confounded by selection over many candidates and by knowledge leakage.
B.motivation: Reframing research-gap identification as a calibrated probabilistic forecast would enable prospective, leakage-free evaluation and would support downstream LLM ideation by ranking gaps with meaningful uncertainty.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework fits a year-sliced topic model on a corpus truncated at year T, scores every unordered topic pair with a temporal gap signal made of recent co-occurrence growth, low saturation, semantic distance, and bibliometric bridge signals, and calibrates that score, using only earlier out-of-sample time splits, into a probability that the pair emerges, defined as crossing a growth threshold, in the window T to T+k. The calibrated scores can then steer an LLM ideator.
B.research_plan: The primary claim is evaluated by backtesting on earlier out-of-sample time splits, comparing the calibrated probabilities against static semantic-distance pairing, trend extrapolation, and graph link-prediction scoring on Brier/log-loss, reliability, and precision@k of emergence, with support required to survive a multiple-comparison correction deflated over candidate pairs and generated ideas. The central failure condition is that the proposed framework does not beat static pairing at fixed rank under the deflated backtest. The secondary claim is evaluated by using the calibrated scores to steer an LLM ideator and rating outputs on grounded novelty, with feasibility held matched.

A.problem: Autonomous research agents automate hypothesis generation, experiment design, and result analysis, but they operate as black boxes, leaving scientists unable to understand why an agent selected a particular hypothesis, designed a specific experiment, or drew a conclusion from data.
A.motivation: Making these systems explainable enables scientists to collaborate with agents rather than blindly trust them, bridging autonomous research automation and explainable AI.
A.proposed_approach: The framework integrates explainability into the core decision-making loops of autonomous research systems. It uses modular agent components with interpretable reasoning traces to produce transparent, real-time justifications for hypothesis selection, experiment design, and result interpretation. The work also designs explanation mechanisms tailored to these research decisions and develops metrics to evaluate explanation fidelity and usefulness.
A.research_plan: The framework is evaluated through empirical evaluation on benchmark tasks and scientist user studies, using the proposed metrics for explanation fidelity and usefulness. The evaluation is intended to support the claim that the framework yields transparent real-time justifications for research decisions; no specific baselines, matched conditions, or failure thresholds are stated.

B.problem: Large language model research agents make critical decisions—selecting hypotheses, designing experiments, choosing analysis methods—but provide no systematic explanations of why they made specific choices; existing trustworthy-agent pipelines and multi-agent interpretation systems do not evaluate whether an agent's explanation is faithful, scientifically sound, and actionable.
B.motivation: Agents are already used for consequential research decisions, and adapting mature XAI evaluation methodology to this setting would let scientists understand, trust, and improve the reasoning behind those decisions.
B.proposed_approach: A framework that generates natural-language justifications for research decisions (hypothesis selection, experiment design, method choice) and evaluates them using three complementary metrics: reasoning fidelity (does the explanation reflect the agent's decision process), scientific soundness (alignment with domain principles and literature), and actionability (usability for understanding, trusting, and improving reasoning). It is instantiated on a curated benchmark of 200–300 research decisions extracted from published studies and validated by domain experts; the evaluation compares multiple baseline agents and ablates explanation components.
B.research_plan: Evidence is an evaluation on a curated benchmark of 200–300 research decisions extracted from published studies and validated by domain experts. Multiple baseline agents are evaluated and explanation components are ablated; the abstract does not specify the named baselines, metric thresholds, or what is held matched. No failure conditions are stated.

A.problem: Current autonomous AI scientist systems rely predominantly on text-based reasoning and language models, leaving rich visual and multimodal data in scientific research underexploited.
A.motivation: Modern scientific research is characterized by visual and multimodal data such as microscopy images, spectroscopy plots, and tabular results; exploiting these data could improve automated hypothesis generation and experimental design.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework integrates vision-language models with structured reasoning to automate hypothesis formation and experiment planning from raw scientific data, including microscopy images, spectroscopy plots, and tabular results. The agent architecture grounds textual hypotheses in visual evidence extracted from scientific images. It uses multimodal chain-of-reasoning to design experiments that bridge visual observations and theoretical predictions. An accompanying evaluation benchmark is provided on real biology and materials science research workflows combining vision, text, and domain knowledge.
A.research_plan: The evidence is an evaluation on a curated dataset of real biology and materials science experiments, comparing the proposed multimodal agent against text-only baselines on hypothesis quality and experimental rigor. The benchmark combines vision, text, and domain knowledge across real workflows.

B.problem: Autonomous AI agents can generate code and execute experiments but struggle to interpret experimental results and use those results to drive iterative discovery.
B.motivation: Closing the interpretation-to-next-experiment loop would allow autonomous agents to move beyond single experiments and support iterative scientific discovery.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is a multimodal agent system that analyzes scientific results including plots, tables, images, and instrument readouts, then generates both interpretations and follow-up experiments. It reasons over visual and tabular outcomes, proposes data-driven hypotheses, and recommends the next experimental design.
B.research_plan: The system will be evaluated on a benchmark of real multi-step scientific workflows spanning chemistry, biology, and materials science, measuring interpretation accuracy and the scientific soundness of proposed next steps. The benchmark serves as evidence for both the interpretation capability and the quality of follow-up experiment recommendations.

A.problem: Current agentic and embodied systems, as they move from oracle-style task competence to tool-using and embodied agency, produce failure modes that cascade—tool misuse, unsafe exploration, goal drift, runaway optimization—rather than remaining isolated errors.
A.motivation: Addressing this now is urgent because these cascading failures undermine the trustworthiness of discovery-oriented systems, and the shift to tool use and embodiment makes such failures increasingly likely.
A.proposed_approach: The work proposes a regulatory specification with risk bands, hard constraints, budgets, uncertainty gating, and checkpoint/rollback, applied to two instantiations: a tool-using research agent and a mobile manipulator using runtime-assurance switching with a conservative safe mode. It maps telemetry to control posture through a single scalar restraint signal. Learned judges and critics are treated as telemetry, not authorities, with the share of abstaining or tied judgments used as an uncertainty signal that tightens posture where no verifier exists. It also distinguishes the ability to perform assigned tasks from the capacity for self-directed model revision and outlines minimal tests for revision triggered by contradictions.
A.research_plan: (1) The two instantiations—a tool-using research agent and a mobile manipulator with runtime-assurance switching—serve as design illustrations for the regulatory specification. (2) Minimal tests are outlined for contradiction-driven model revision, supporting the claim that task performance and self-directed revision are distinct. (3) The abstract states no baselines, metrics, failure conditions, or matched quantities for empirical validation.

B.problem: Autonomous research agents are judged mainly by final outputs such as papers or recovered equations, but the epistemic process of revising a stated belief when evidence contradicts it is not directly measured.
B.motivation: Directly measuring belief updating would reveal whether output-competent AI-scientist systems are epistemically unreliable, preventing misplaced trust in autonomous research agents.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark and instrumentation protocol measures whether an AI-scientist system's expressed commitment to a hypothesis moves in the correct direction, by the correct amount, and substantively rather than merely verbally as controlled evidence arrives. It builds agent-relative evidence schedules aimed at disconfirming the agent's own reported hypothesis and scores the resulting belief trajectory against a computable Bayesian reference. The protocol specifies four quantitative metrics and five ground-truth environments, with baselines including an explicit-statistical inference agent.
B.research_plan: (1) The central claim is tested by running state-of-the-art scaffolds through the proposed protocol across five ground-truth environments, scoring their belief trajectories with four quantitative metrics and comparing against a computable Bayesian reference and baselines including an explicit-statistical inference agent. The evidence would support the claim if scaffolds show conservative or vacuous revision under disconfirmation even when they terminate at the correct hypothesis; it would fail if belief trajectories revise correctly and substantively under the same disconfirmation. The abstract does not specify exact thresholds, matched compute or parameter budgets, or which metrics serve as primary endpoints.

A.problem: AI-scientist systems now produce complete papers end-to-end, but independent evaluations show that a large fraction of their experimental results are fabricated, invalidated, or unsupported, and existing benchmarks score the final manuscript as a whole, so they cannot say which stage causes failure.
A.motivation: Stage attribution would let interventions target the failing component, and artifact-grounded auditing offers a route to more trustworthy AI-scientist output.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed stage-decomposed evaluation and audit stack has two components. The first is a suite of about 40 fully specified research protocols—each fixing question, data, baseline, metric, seed, and acceptance criteria—where the idea is held fixed and only the implementation agent is varied across a strong coding agent, an intermediate research scaffold, a weak single-pass LLM, and a human-calibrated reference; the same writer LLM drafts a manuscript from each run's artifacts. The second is a post-hoc, system-agnostic auditor that extracts every quantitative claim from a manuscript and grades each as Supported, Contradicted, Unsupported, or Unverifiable against execution artifacts, using programmatic recomputation where feasible. Audit verdicts can be fed back into the agent loop.
A.research_plan: The plan evaluates each falsifiable claim. (1) For the attribution claim, the benchmark holds the research protocols fixed, swaps implementation agents, and uses the same writer LLM to generate manuscripts; variance in the claim-valid proportion is compared across the implementer, idea, and writing stages, with the idea fixed and writing held constant as specified. (2) For the auditor claim, the auditor grades every extracted quantitative claim against execution artifacts, using programmatic recomputation where possible, and its detection F1 for unsupported and contradicted claims is compared with text-only LLM auditing on the same manuscripts. (3) For the reviewer/feedback claim, off-the-shelf LLM reviewer judgments are correlated with the claim-valid proportion, and audit verdicts are fed back into the agent loop to measure reduction in invalid claims. Each claim is falsifiable: the attribution claim fails if implementer choice does not drive most variance; the auditing claim fails if artifact-grounded auditing does not outperform text-only auditing; the feedback claim fails if reviewer correlation is strong or feedback does not reduce invalid claims.

B.problem: Current evaluation of end-to-end AI scientist systems relies on peer-review or AI-reviewer scores, but this evaluation stack does not check whether the quantitative claims in a generated paper are supported by its own experimental artifacts.
B.motivation: As AI scientist systems increasingly produce complete manuscripts and are judged by review scores, unsupported quantitative claims can pass as sound; auditing the final paper and repository is needed to assess the property that actually matters.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed post-hoc audit protocol and benchmark extracts every quantitative claim from an AI-generated paper, maps each claim to executable units in the committed repository, re-executes those units in a deterministic sandbox, and issues a typed claim-level verdict—SUPPORTED / UNSUPPORTED / UNVERIFIABLE—with an error taxonomy covering fabricated numbers, seed cherry-picks, misread tables, and wrong metrics. The benchmark applies this protocol across at least three open AI scientist system classes (AI Scientist-v2-class, Jr. AI Scientist-class, InternAgent-class).
B.research_plan: (1) For the weak-correlation claim, the paper compares peer-review and AI-reviewer scores against the supported-claim fraction across the benchmarked AI scientist systems; support is a weak correlation and failure is a strong correlation. (2) For detection performance, it runs the re-execution auditor on extracted claims, calibrates the false-positive rate on injected errors, and compares against paper-only and log-only LLM auditors; support requires detecting a non-trivial fraction of unsupported claims at bounded false positives, and failure is no improvement or an unbounded false-positive rate. (3) For the feedback claim, it feeds audit verdicts back to writer/experiment agents and measures both the supported-claim fraction and review scores; support is an increase in the supported-claim fraction with no decrease in review scores.

A.problem: Efficient and adaptive hypothesis generation in evolutionary algorithms remains an open challenge, particularly for discovering superior hypotheses in complex search spaces.
A.motivation: Large language models can generate and refine hypotheses, and reinforcement learning provides optimization capabilities; combining these with evolutionary search may make hypothesis generation more efficient and tractable for complex optimization problems.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework combines evolutionary search with LLM-generated and RL-refined hypotheses: LLMs generate and refine candidate hypotheses, RL optimizes the hypothesis generation process, and evolutionary search provides exploration. The approach is applied to various optimization problems and compared against traditional evolutionary algorithms and LLM-based methods.
A.research_plan: The evidence is comparative evaluation on various optimization problems, with performance compared against traditional evolutionary algorithms and LLM-based methods.

B.problem: Existing LLM-based automated heuristic design treats algorithm evolution as a monolithic text generation task, overlooking the coupling between discrete algorithmic structures and continuous numerical parameters; consequently, promising algorithms are often discarded due to uncalibrated constants, and premature convergence arises from simple similarity metrics.
B.motivation: By decoupling structural reasoning from parameter optimization, it becomes possible to retain promising algorithms that would otherwise be discarded and to avoid premature convergence, thereby enabling more effective automated heuristic design for combinatorial optimization.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is a tuning-integrated dynamic evolution system with a nested architecture. An outer parallel island model uses a tree similarity edit distance to maintain structural diversity across evolving heuristics. An inner loop integrates LLM-based logic generation with a differential mutation operator for parameter tuning. A UCB-based scheduler dynamically prioritizes high-yield prompt strategies to allocate resources.
B.research_plan: Extensive experiments across nine combinatorial optimization problems compare the proposed framework against state-of-the-art baselines on solution quality, search efficiency, and computational cost. The abstract does not specify metrics, datasets, ablated components, or failure conditions.

A.problem: Existing LLM agents for autonomous scientific discovery face bottlenecks in generating correct, executable, and reproducible research code. These agents largely rely on reactive debugging from compiler errors or raw execution traces and lack structured internal verification.
A.motivation: Structured internal verification inspired by human cognitive workflows and test-driven development may avoid cascading logic errors and make scientific discovery code more robust end-to-end.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed agentic framework connects natural language research hypotheses to robust code execution by synthesizing automated test cases, verifying a step-by-step plan through simulation prior to code generation, and iterating through hierarchical multi-turn feedback loops. It is applied to scientific code generation tasks.
A.research_plan: The evaluation design applies the framework to scientific code benchmarks and compares it with existing reactive-debugging agents. Claim (1) is assessed by whether cascading logic errors are systematically reduced; claim (2) by whether end-to-end scientific discovery performance improves. The abstract does not specify named baselines, metrics, matching conditions, or failure thresholds.

B.problem: Scientific code generation with LLMs is unreliable, suffers from error propagation in multi-agent workflows, and lacks dependable evaluation in domains with ill-defined success metrics.
B.motivation: Automating scientific code generation could reduce manual coding burden, but reliable use requires better coordination and evaluation, and non-coding practitioners need a way to express domain needs without manual prompt engineering.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed platform coordinates three LLM-based agents under a Bayesian framework: a planning agent structures user inputs into actionable plans and adaptive test cases, a code-generating agent produces candidate solutions, and an evaluator agent provides comprehensive feedback. In an adversarial loop, the planning agent iteratively refines test cases to challenge the code-generating agent, while prompt distributions are dynamically updated using Bayesian principles and code quality metrics, including functional correctness, structural alignment, and static analysis. The platform also translates non-expert prompts into domain-specific requirements, bypassing manual prompt engineering for practitioners without coding backgrounds.
B.research_plan: The evidence consists of benchmark evaluations intended to assess robust code generation and error propagation, and testing on a cross-disciplinary Earth Science task against competing models. The abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, ablations, or failure conditions.

A.problem: Most current LLM-based symbolic regression methods are passive: they evaluate fixed, static datasets rather than choosing which experiments to run next.
A.motivation: Actively selecting informative experiments, as human scientists do, could reduce the number of experiments needed to discover interpretable equations and help disambiguate competing hypotheses.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed LLM-based autonomous agent maintains a population of candidate equations, computes information gain and expected model disagreement to identify the next most informative experiment, and iteratively refines hypotheses through a closed feedback loop. It actively proposes which experiment to run next instead of evaluating a fixed dataset.
A.research_plan: On synthetic symbolic regression benchmarks, the agent is compared with passive baselines; the evidence is whether it recovers ground-truth equations with fewer experiments and high symbolic accuracy. A failure would be no reduction in experiments or a drop in accuracy relative to passive baselines.

B.problem: Existing approaches recover governing ordinary differential equations as a static inference problem over fixed datasets, assuming observed trajectories are sufficiently informative; when data are limited, multiple equations can be observationally indistinguishable, creating identifiability gaps and incorrect recovered equations.
B.motivation: Adaptive data acquisition can resolve observational indistinguishability, and large language models make tractable priors over large equation spaces, enabling correct recovery from limited and noisy data.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed closed-loop framework jointly optimizes symbolic hypothesis construction and adaptive data acquisition. A large language model proposes operator priors that partition the large search space into distinct regions, and candidate equations within each region are fit to observed data. Disagreement among the candidates guides acquisition of informative trajectories, forming a feedback loop that iteratively refines both the hypothesis space and the discovered dynamics.
B.research_plan: Evidence for claim (1) comes from evaluation on 122 ODE systems spanning ODEBench and ODEBase, using median NMSE and symbolic accuracy against state-of-the-art baselines. Claim (2) is assessed through sample-efficiency analysis comparing performance under reduced data fractions. Claim (3) is tested by noise-robustness analysis and comparison of recovered symbolic structures, checking for spurious terms relative to baselines.

A.problem: The paper-centric review system cannot adequately assess research rigor and reproducibility, and autonomous AI agents that generate large volumes of research outputs make this scalability and rigor problem worse.
A.motivation: Automated research evaluators become necessary to keep pace with AI-generated outputs and to move beyond narrative review toward more rigorous, reproducible scientific practice.
A.proposed_approach: The work develops an automated AI-agent evaluation framework that examines code and data along with the paper, rather than relying only on narrative review. It uses mechanistic interpretability research as a testbed and builds standardized research outputs for evaluation. The framework assesses the coherence of the experimental process, the reproducibility of results, and the generalizability of findings.
A.research_plan: (1) To support the evaluation-quality claim, the authors compare the framework's judgments with human judges on standardized mechanistic interpretability research outputs, treating agreement as the success criterion. (2) To support the claim that it surfaces issues beyond human review, they compare the issues the framework identifies against issues found by human reviewers; failure would be poor agreement or failure to surface additional reviewer-missed issues.

B.problem: Current research-agent benchmarks ask only whether an agent can make an experiment run and reproduce a target number, which is inadequate for empirical research where a study can execute perfectly yet still be invalid due to wrong statistical test, temporal-slice leakage, uncontrolled confounders, or post-hoc selection.
B.motivation: Assessing and improving agents on methodological validity matters because empirical studies can be invalid despite successful execution; a benchmark with protocol-level ground truth and automatic fidelity checking makes it possible to evaluate and repair this axis rather than optimizing execution alone.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark reconstructs tasks from real published empirical software-engineering studies—repository/GitHub mining, defect prediction, code-review and commit analyses—each shipped with its data, a research question, and its methodological protocol as the ground-truth standard. Evaluation has two axes: execution success (the pipeline runs and produces results) and methodological fidelity, scored by an automatic verifier that combines programmatic checks for statistical-test choice, temporal train/test slicing, multiple-testing correction, and seed/data provenance with a protocol-grounded LLM rubric for confounders/controls, effect-size reporting, and selection bias. The construction pipeline and verifier are specified, and a repair loop uses the verifier's feedback to update agent-generated studies.
B.research_plan: Evidence for the first two claims comes from running four agent frameworks on the benchmark tasks and scoring both execution success and methodological fidelity, then testing whether execution success predicts validity; the claims would fail if agents showed high fidelity or if execution success tracked validity. Evidence for the repair-loop claim compares end-to-end valid-study rate when verifier feedback is added against execution-feedback-only baselines, with frameworks and tasks held matched; it would fail without a significant advantage. Ablations isolate the rigor axis from the execution axis.

A.problem: Existing work has diagnosed an implementation gap in end-to-end AI scientist systems—they frequently fail to execute rigorous experiments—but no retrieved work measures a second downstream failure: a large fraction of the quantitative claims in the final manuscript are unsupported or contradicted by the raw experiment artifacts the same agent generated.
A.motivation: As end-to-end AI scientists now produce complete papers, unsupported quantitative claims can enter the literature uncorrected because post-hoc LLM review demonstrably fails to catch unsupported numbers and faulty logic, and execution-level governance frameworks verify tasks but never the manuscript.
A.proposed_approach: The work proposes two components. The first is a protocol that extracts every falsifiable quantitative claim from AI-scientist papers, maps each claim to a machine-checkable specification over the agent's own logs, metrics, and code, and has an independent, read-only, cross-model auditor re-execute the checks. The second is a verification-gated writing loop in which the scientist registers each falsifiable claim with its check specification before writing, an independent auditor verifies each check against raw artifacts, and the writer is hard-constrained to report only auditor-supported claims, demoting all others to explicit hypothesis framing.
A.research_plan: The evidence is empirical: the protocol measures baseline unsupported-claim rates and their orthogonality to implementation success in AI-scientist-generated papers; the loop is then evaluated against the baseline on unsupported-claim and contradiction rates, while implementation success and reviewer-assessed paper quality are assessed for preservation. Failure conditions implied by the predictions are that baseline rates are not high or not orthogonal, the loop does not reduce the rates, or implementation/quality is not preserved.

B.problem: Autonomous AI-scientist systems produce papers whose claims routinely outrun their evidence—hallucinated numerical results, misused metrics, and data leakage that final-manuscript inspection misses—yet existing review components are deployed only as post-hoc acceptance predictors or external scoring metrics, not as a controller that changes what the scientist does.
B.motivation: Making review an active controller would target verifiable claim–evidence alignment during generation rather than after the fact, and would turn reviewer noise from an assumed condition into a measured confound.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed architecture has a reviewer agent and an author agent iterate over a shared claim–evidence ledger: claims carry stable ids, evidence is bound to executed run records, critiques must resolve to a claim id plus an evidence id or 'unsupported', and author responses must be a discrete machine-checkable action—run a new experiment, revise a claim, withdraw a claim, or rebut with cited existing evidence. A pre-dispatch precision gate admits only critiques whose references resolve to finished artifacts. The authors also contribute a paired counterfactual benchmark in which the same author agent runs the same AI-research tasks (EXP-Bench, AutoExperiment) with and without the loop, and the delta is decomposed into claim support, critique precision/recall, experimental validity, held-out reviewer acceptance, and cost.
B.research_plan: (1) The first claim—improvement on verifiable scientific quality over no reviewer, single-shot self-critique, and writing-only critique—is tested through the paired counterfactual benchmark, with the same author agent running the same tasks with and without the loop and with verifiable quality measured as the fraction of claims backed by passing executed experiments and a validity audit. (2) The second claim—that the gain requires both the grounding constraint and the precision gate—is assessed through the benchmark's decomposition into claim support, critique precision/recall, experimental validity, held-out reviewer acceptance, and cost; if measured gains appear only in fluency or reviewer-score metrics, the claim is treated as false and reported as a negative result.

A.problem: Rigorous real-world physical research using large language models is stalled by a lack of realistic evaluation benchmarks and by systemic LLM hallucinations.
A.motivation: Addressing these barriers would make automated scientific discovery in quantum many-body simulation more robust, reliable, and transparent.
A.proposed_approach: The work releases a research-level benchmark of 100 tasks in quantum many-body simulation drawn from 21 high-impact journals. The proposed framework is a multi-agent system that enforces self-verification and error correction; it integrates programming verifiers and scientific verifiers to check coding correctness and principle-based physical validity, producing interpretable evidence and error correction at each step.
A.research_plan: (1) The claim that the benchmark is research-level and challenging rests on its construction from 100 tasks in 21 high-impact journals and on testing against current frontier LLMs. (2) The claim that the framework enforces reliable, physically valid outputs rests on comparisons with existing LLM baselines across benchmark scenarios and on evaluation of inference-time scaling.

B.problem: Current language agents in autonomous AI scientist systems frequently fail during complex, multi-step experimental execution and validation because they lack adequate error correction and rigorous intermediate verification; this produces an implementation gap between generated research plans and executable, validated results.
B.motivation: As autonomous scientist systems become more capable at generating hypotheses, code, and reports, trustworthy adoption depends on closing the implementation gap so that agent-produced work is executable and its conclusions reliable.
B.proposed_approach: The framework integrates constraint-guided test-time verification and dynamic self-correction loops into autonomous scientific workflows. Scientific verification is decomposed into domain-specific invariant checking, automated test case synthesis, and executable code validation. Test-time interaction and verification compute are scaled to catch errors before conclusions are finalized.
B.research_plan: The comparative claim is evaluated on challenging scientific agent benchmarks against standard prompting and unverified iterative debugging baselines, measuring execution success rates and reliability of discovered findings. The detection claim is addressed through the framework's decomposition into invariant checking, test synthesis, and code validation, though no explicit failure condition or ablation is stated.

A.problem: Business process discovery is currently framed as automatically mining a single process model from event logs, leaving competing structural and control-flow explanations ungenerated and unvalidated.
A.motivation: Recent LLM-based agentic systems make it feasible to automate hypothesis generation, simulation, conformance checking, and iterative refinement, turning discovery from one-shot model extraction into an autonomous research process.
A.proposed_approach: The system uses an LLM-based multi-agent framework: agents generate competing hypotheses about process structure, bottlenecks, and control-flow alternatives from event logs; candidate process models embodying these hypotheses are designed and simulated; models are validated through conformance checking and performance prediction; and the system iterates autonomously to refine and rank hypotheses by evidence strength. The proposed system will be implemented and evaluated on real-world event logs.
A.research_plan: The evaluation will be on real-world event logs and will compare hypothesis quality, model fit, and actionable insights against traditional process mining baselines and human domain expert assessment. This evidence would support the core capability claim if the system autonomously generates, validates, refines, and evidence-ranks process hypotheses; failure would be indicated by inability to produce or meaningfully rank hypotheses.

B.problem: Current large language models and autonomous AI research agents lack mechanisms to perform fully unsupervised discovery of business process models directly from event logs and organizational data; existing LLM-based process mining and workflow generation approaches either require human feedback loops or focus on documentation rather than automated discovery.
B.motivation: Fully autonomous discovery would remove human-in-the-loop effort and could surface process variants and anomalies that supervised approaches miss.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is a self-orchestrating multi-agent system in which LLM agents autonomously discover, formalize, and validate process models from raw event logs through iterative hypothesis generation, statistical validation, and process documentation, without human intervention. The agent system performs automated experiment planning via data sampling and conformance testing, selects process mining techniques, and forms scientific hypotheses to identify optimal process structures.
B.research_plan: The framework is evaluated on synthetic and real-world event logs; the evaluation compares autonomous discovery against human-guided process mining and assesses whether the framework identifies process variants and anomalies that supervised approaches miss. The abstract does not state explicit metrics or failure conditions.

A.problem: Autonomous AI Scientist systems are currently evaluated on reviewer scores, task completion, and experimental-information diagnostics, but not on whether the positive findings they report are actually true.
A.motivation: Scientific value ultimately rests on whether reported positive findings are true, so there is a need to make spurious discovery the headline metric and to determine where verification compute should actually be spent; oracle environments with known executable ground truth make such measurement tractable.
A.proposed_approach: An oracle-based benchmark runs full discovery loops inside environments whose executable ground truth is known, including matched control environments in which no true effect exists, so every reported positive is spurious by construction. Claim veracity is decided automatically by re-executing each reported claim's own code against freshly drawn oracle data under multiple-testing corrections. On top of this measurement layer, an independent execution-enabled adversarial refuter has the sole reward of falsifying a candidate claim before it may be reported; it is compared against a proposer-only pipeline, a self-critique pipeline, and different fractions of compute allocated to refutation.
A.research_plan: Evidence for the measurement layer is the benchmark's construction: full discovery loops, known executable ground truth, matched control environments with no true effect, and automatic re-execution with multiple-testing corrections. The central claim about adversarial refutation gating is tested by comparing the proposed refuter pipeline against the proposer-only and self-critique pipelines and across different compute fractions, while holding total compute fixed. The comparison uses oracle-measured false-discovery rate and verified discovery yield; a failure condition is that the refutation-gated pipeline does not lower false-discovery rate relative to baselines, does not retain a large share of yield, or that text-only self-critique lowers it similarly.

B.problem: End-to-end AI Scientist systems organize discovery almost entirely as greedy improvement seeking, discarding or under-reporting null and negative outcomes. Independent evaluations connect this design to overgeneralized, fragile, and occasionally fabricated claims, while existing falsification-oriented systems either run falsification outside the discovery loop or validate externally supplied hypotheses rather than steering an ongoing search.
B.motivation: Treating refutation as a scarce in-loop resource may avoid the documented fragile and overgeneralized claims, and a controller plus a benchmark with verifiable ground truth outside the search distribution makes the design hypothesis testable now.
B.proposed_approach: At each step, a drop-in controller spends a budget fraction α on actively chosen refutation trials: configurations where the current claim is most likely to be contradicted. Failures gate candidate adoption, re-scope claims to the empirically supported regime, and seed the next falsification target. The paper also introduces a benchmark of regime-structured discovery tasks with verifiable ground truth outside the search distribution.
B.research_plan: (1) The central hypothesis is tested by comparing a positive falsification allocation against the α = 0 greedy baseline at matched total experiment cost, with validity and calibration of claims per unit experiment budget as the evaluation target. (2) A pre-specified null finding would indicate that experiment-budget composition is not the bottleneck identified in current failure analyses and would argue against falsification-centric redesigns. The proposed benchmark of regime-structured discovery tasks with verifiable ground truth outside the search distribution provides the evaluation setting.

A.problem: Current benchmarks assess LLM research agents' ideation, structuring, and execution, but none measures the intervening decision of which candidate hypothesis to test next under a finite budget, leaving cost-aware hypothesis selection unmeasured.
A.motivation: When experiments have heterogeneous costs and the objective is the best experimentally confirmed hypothesis rather than cumulative confirmations, policies that optimize cumulative confirmation can over-invest in cheap mediocre hypotheses and under-invest in expensive high-yield ones, making selection under budget a decisive bottleneck.
A.proposed_approach: The approach defines an execution-based benchmark and a falsifiable theory of the discovery loop. It specifies a discovery objective as the best experimentally confirmed hypothesis (discovery yield), heterogeneous experiment costs, a reward and cost model, and a set of baseline policies spanning portfolio/bandit and agentic methods. Metrics include discovery yield, yield-per-cost, selection regret against an omniscient bound, and false-confirmation rate, with environment suites and a five-way ablation plan.
A.research_plan: (1) To test the max-K claim, compare a cost-aware max-K-armed bandit policy against cumulative-confirmation policies in the budget-scarce regime, measuring discovery yield, yield-per-cost, and selection regret against an omniscient bound. (2) To test the fabrication-gate claim, vary fabrication rate and compare a cheap falsification gate against no gate, measuring false-confirmation rate and yield-per-cost below and above the threshold. (3) Use five-way ablations to isolate the component(s) a claim credits. The falsifiable design accepts either a negative or positive result as deciding whether objective-matched (max-K) or falsification-gated selection should replace cumulative-reward training, with baselines and metrics held matched where trade-offs are compared.

B.problem: Across AI-driven science, generative capacity has outpaced investigative judgment: it is now possible to produce millions of plausible candidates in hours, but not yet to decide which of them merit expensive validation.
B.motivation: This asymmetry is described as the central bottleneck of scientific discovery for the next decade; resolving it is necessary to convert generative capacity into scientific progress without wasting expensive validation.
B.proposed_approach: The paper formalizes the principle as a multi-fidelity Markov decision process in which agents maximize the value of information purchased relative to its cost; the formulation is pluralistic, admitting reinforcement learning, evolutionary algorithms, and multi-armed bandits. The framework is developed in protein design, where the vendor hierarchy runs from sequence embeddings to wet-lab assays and spans several orders of magnitude, and the same structure is argued to recur in materials science and autonomous chemistry. Three grand challenges concerning cross-modal calibration, asynchronous decision logic, and interpretable strategy are proposed as anchors for a 2030 benchmark.
B.research_plan: The paper's evidence is its conceptual framing and formalization, together with the claimed recurrence of the same structure across protein design, materials science, and autonomous chemistry. Progress is anchored by a 2030 benchmark whose success condition is an agent discovering a functional protein at 1% of the compute and 10% of the lab cost of human-designed pipelines; failure is falling short of that target. The three grand challenges are proposed as criteria for tracking progress, but the abstract does not specify concrete experiments or ablations.

A.problem: Autonomous research agents produce competitive solutions and professional-looking manuscripts, yet their outputs contain verifiability failures—fabricated citations, unreproducible scores, and method descriptions that diverge from the implementation—that surface-level evaluation cannot detect.
A.motivation: Hidden verifiability failures undermine trust in autonomous research outputs, and the growing capability of such agents makes a uniform way to trace evidence and audit integrity timely.
A.proposed_approach: The work consists of three components. First, a verifiability framework requires every claim to be traceable to its evidence source. Second, an end-to-end autonomous research system maintains such evidence chains by construction throughout literature review, solution discovery, and paper writing. Third, a post-hoc audit applies four integrity checks—score verification, specification violation, reference verification, and method-code alignment—uniformly to any system's outputs.
A.research_plan: The paper applies the four integrity checks to 75 papers produced by five systems across five frontier research tasks to characterize verifiability failures. The proposed system is assessed with the same checks on the five tasks, and its outputs are compared with human expert performance.
