Generalization is tested on six additional tasks spanning medical imaging, fine-grained recognition, 3D perception, and language modeling, including the Parameter Golf and MLE-Bench benchmarks, with baselines for comparison. No independent failure threshold is stated beyond the audit checks themselves.

B.problem: Existing peer-review evaluation tools for AI-generated manuscripts rely solely on text inspection or generic LLM evaluations, leaving them blind to internal discrepancies between textual claims and ground-truth execution artifacts such as code execution logs and quantitative artifact logs.
B.motivation: Bridging this gap would preserve scientific integrity in fully automated discovery pipelines by enabling empirical claims to be verified against actual execution artifacts.
B.proposed_approach: A multi-agent framework programmatically and semantically cross-verifies empirical claims in AI-generated manuscripts against immutable execution traces, raw MLflow/artifact logs, and reproducibility pipelines. It extracts explicit quantitative assertions from manuscript text, maps them to corresponding execution run IDs and code blocks using structured lineage tracking, and flags inconsistencies.
B.research_plan: The proposed framework is evaluated on benchmark suites of AI-generated papers by comparing its detection of manuscript-execution inconsistencies against text-only peer review and baseline hallucination detectors.

A.problem: Current multi-agent LLM frameworks for hypothesis generation in disease diagnosis and drug discovery have room for improvement in integrating domain-specific knowledge, standardizing evaluation benchmarks, and scaling hypothesis generation.
A.motivation: Accelerating hypothesis generation through multi-agent LLMs could advance disease diagnosis and drug discovery, and existing frameworks make this approach tractable to build on.
A.proposed_approach: A multi-agent LLM framework for biomedical hypothesis generation that builds on existing frameworks and focuses on improved integration of domain-specific knowledge, standardized evaluation benchmarks, and scalable hypothesis generation.
A.research_plan: The framework will be validated through extensive experimentation and case studies in real-world biomedical applications; the abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, ablations, or failure conditions.

B.problem: The rapid growth of biomedical knowledge has outpaced our ability to efficiently extract insights and generate novel hypotheses.
B.motivation: Large Language Models have emerged as promising tools to revolutionize knowledge interaction and potentially accelerate biomedical discovery, making autonomous hypothesis generation and experiment design tractable.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework uses LLM agents to autonomously generate hypotheses and design experiments in medical research, grounded in large datasets and existing literature. It incorporates multi-agent systems and self-evaluation mechanisms to improve novelty and relevance of generated hypotheses. It will be applied in specific medical domains, and evaluation metrics will be developed to assess effectiveness.
B.research_plan: The proposal states that the framework will be evaluated in specific medical domains with newly developed evaluation metrics, but does not specify baselines, failure conditions, or what is held matched.

A.problem: Existing frameworks for AI scientists and LLM-based research assistants rely on static tool suites or single-shot self-debugging when encountering domain-specific computational challenges, limiting their ability to discover, synthesize, and verify complex scientific software modules such as specialized simulation solvers and advanced evaluation pipelines.
A.motivation: Recent advancements in autonomous AI scientists and LLM-based research assistants make it feasible to automate stages of the scientific process, but dynamic construction of domain-specific toolkits remains needed to support complex downstream discovery.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework integrates execution-guided tree search with automated program synthesis. It treats scientific software generation as an open-ended search problem over code syntax and execution feedback, iteratively discovering modular tools that can be built, tested, and refined for downstream scientific use.
A.research_plan: Evidence consists of evaluations across multi-discipline scientific discovery benchmarks, comparing the proposed method against static-tool and linear self-correction baselines on code correctness and empirical discovery outcomes. The abstract does not describe ablations, matched resource controls, or an explicit failure condition.

B.problem: The central challenge for AI in science is not reasoning alone but the ability to create computational methods in an open-ended scientific world. Existing LLM-based agents rely on static, pre-defined tool libraries, which fails where scientific tools are sparse, heterogeneous, and intrinsically incomplete.
B.motivation: Enabling agents to create tools as problem-driven artifacts during inference would remove the rigidity and long-tail limitations of fixed tool libraries.
B.proposed_approach: The authors propose an inference-time paradigm in which an agent synthesizes, verifies, and evolves executable tools as problem-driven artifacts rather than selecting from a fixed tool library. They also construct a benchmark of 1,590 scientific reasoning tasks supported by 925 automatically evolved tools, and release the code and benchmark.
B.research_plan: The paper evaluates the paradigm on the released benchmark of scientific reasoning tasks and automatically evolved tools, measuring accuracy, tool efficiency, and cross-domain adaptation of computational tools. The abstract does not name the compared baseline systems or specify failure conditions.

A.problem: Autonomous AI scientist systems produce unreliable conclusions—experiments fail to run, results are fabricated or invalidated, and failures such as data leakage, metric misuse, and post-hoc selection bias escape detection. The dominant verification mechanism, self-critique by the same model that produced the claim, is structurally incapable of locating its own errors.
A.motivation: As AI scientist systems increasingly produce research, an independent mechanism that can invalidate unreliable claims before they are accepted is needed to make their conclusions trustworthy.
A.proposed_approach: An independent tool-using auditor agent is explicitly incentivized to refute an AI scientist's claim by attacking its evidence chain: requesting new control conditions, swapping splits, probing for leakage, and challenging metric choices, with every objection backed by an executable experiment rather than prose. The evaluation uses a benchmark of research tasks with planted fragilities and known ground truth, built from synthetic tasks with known data-generating processes and curator-validated tasks from real open-source ML papers. The benchmark measures how robust a conclusion is to adversarial audit.
A.research_plan: (1) The audit protocol is compared against self-critique and a fair independent reviewer on a benchmark of research tasks with planted fragilities and known ground truth, using the rate at which planted-false claims are overturned as the main evidence for the first claim. (2) Claims surviving each mechanism are compared against ground truth to test whether survival tracks validity. (3) The protocol is checked for overcorrection by whether it also rejects genuine effects. A stated failure condition is that if adversarial audit adds nothing over the alternatives or merely flips everything, the hypothesis is rejected.

B.problem: End-to-end AI Scientist systems (AI Scientist-v2, Jr. AI Scientist, Kosmos, Co-Scientist) rely on an in-loop reviewer that shares the proposer's context, evidence, and acceptance goal; existing benchmarks (SPOT, FLAWS, BadScientist) find that LLM verifiers fail to detect fabricated or flawed claims, but it is unknown how much of this failure is model capability versus verification architecture.
B.motivation: If verification architecture rather than model capability drives these failures, AI-scientist integrators must change quality control; instrumented execution logs and hash-chained ground truth now make it possible to test epistemic independence without LLM judgment.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed audit layer withholds the proposer's hidden trajectory, candidate runs, and self-critique behind an information firewall; forces the auditor into an adversarial falsification goal ('assume each claim is false; find the contradiction') rather than a scoring goal; and anchors every claim to an execution-log-derived claim-evidence registry (which run, script, split, and metric, or NULL if none). To test it, the paper proposes a benchmark of roughly 110 instrumented AI-scientist-produced papers, clean plus sabotaged by five automation-specific failure modes, with claim-level ground truth defined by hash-chained execution logs rather than LLM judgment.
B.research_plan: (1) The benchmark's clean and sabotaged papers are labeled at claim level from hash-chained execution logs, so ground truth does not depend on LLM judgment. (2) Evaluation compares the proposed independent falsification-role auditor against the proposer's own self-review and acceptance-oriented reviewers, holding evidence constant and measuring claim-level recall of injected flaws. (3) An ablation varies role separation, registry access, and adversarial framing to quantify their separate contributions to detection. (4) The failure condition for the architecture claim is that role separation adds nothing over evidence/registry access; if so, verification remains purely an evidence problem, whereas a positive role-separation effect would mean the in-loop critic cannot serve as the final judge of its own claims.

A.problem: Current AI research systems cannot reliably translate natural-language scientific hypotheses into verifiable experimental designs, leaving them unable to validate that a proposed experiment actually tests the stated hypothesis.
A.motivation: This is a critical bottleneck for autonomous AI scientists: without formal validation, autonomous systems cannot be trusted to run experiments that address the claims they set out to test.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed system is an NLP and formal-methods pipeline. It parses free-form scientific hypotheses into semantic predicates, generates testable predictions with measurable outcomes, and synthesizes structured experimental protocol specifications. It includes an automated verification stage that checks whether the specified experimental design corresponds to the stated hypothesis.
A.research_plan: The evidence is an evaluation on a corpus of published papers. The proposed pipeline's formalized experimental specifications are compared with LLM-only hypothesis-to-experiment workflows on the detection of design flaws: missing controls, unmeasured variables, and unvalidated predictions. Support requires the formal specification approach to detect more of these flaws than the baseline; failure occurs if it detects no more flaws or fewer. The abstract does not state whether workflows are matched on compute, model, or other protocol-generation conditions.

B.problem: Autonomous AI research agents generate scientific claims at scale but lack rigorous guarantees that their outputs are logically sound and empirically valid.
B.motivation: As such agents now generate claims at scale, machine-checkable evidence could move assurance beyond empirical claim verification and make agent-generated findings trustworthy.
B.proposed_approach: The framework formally specifies scientific validity properties such as statistical power, logical consistency, and reproducibility constraints. AI agents are instrumented to emit proof certificates during execution, and automated theorem proving and model checking are applied to those certificates to produce machine-checkable evidence that the workflow's claims satisfy the specifications. The approach is demonstrated on materials science hypothesis generation and statistical hypothesis testing.
B.research_plan: (1)(2) The evidence consists of demonstrations on materials science hypothesis generation and statistical hypothesis testing. The formal framework is evaluated against existing empirical verifiers. Support for claim (2) requires invalid claims identified by the formal specification that existing empirical verifiers miss; a failure would be the inability to identify such claims. No quantitative metrics or named baselines beyond existing empirical verifiers are specified.

A.problem: Existing LLM-based scientific idea generation methods are limited to computer science and closely related domains, and their applicability to other scientific fields such as data-driven astronomy remains largely underexplored.
A.motivation: The rapid development of scientific discovery demands innovative tools, and recent breakthroughs in generative AI and LLMs offer transformative potential for generating research ideas in data-intensive disciplines like astronomy.
A.proposed_approach: The framework uses LLMs in a human-AI collaborative workflow and integrates four stages: conception, iterative refinement, expert validation, and knowledge integration. It is applied to generate research ideas in data-driven astronomy, where massive telescope and satellite datasets are analyzed with data science methods.
A.research_plan: The paper evaluates the framework through experiments with human expert assessments and model self-evaluation of generated drafts. It compares the framework's generated ideas with human-generated ideas on originality and feasibility across multiple data-driven astronomy topics. For the claim that the framework accelerates discovery cycles, the abstract relies on the same human and model assessments but does not specify an explicit failure condition or matched controls beyond topic coverage.

B.problem: The early stages of scientific research require substantial manual effort for generating hypotheses, and it is not currently established how to automate generation of scientific hypotheses that are novel, relevant, and feasible.
B.motivation: Large language models and large domain-specific scientific paper datasets are now available, making it tractable to develop AI systems that can significantly reduce manual effort and accelerate early-stage research.
B.proposed_approach: Fine-tune a large language model on a large dataset of scientific papers from a specific domain, then use the fine-tuned model to generate hypotheses intended to be novel, relevant, and feasible. The system will be evaluated using a comprehensive framework that integrates automated tools and human judgment to assess the quality of generated hypotheses.
B.research_plan: The evidence consists of evaluating the quality of generated hypotheses using a comprehensive framework that integrates automated tools and human judgment, assessing novelty, relevance, and feasibility. The abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, ablations, or a failure condition for the claimed reduction in manual effort.

A.problem: Single-agent architectures and sequential tool calls in LLM-based HPC workflows become serialization bottlenecks during large-scale simulation campaigns and fail to utilize the massive parallelism of exascale resources.
A.motivation: AI-HPC integration is moving scientific workflows toward adaptive autonomous decision-making, and open-weight LLMs plus exascale resources now make scalable autonomous orchestration tractable and broadly useful.
A.proposed_approach: A central planning agent dynamically partitions workloads and assigns subtasks to a swarm of parallel executor agents. All executor agents interface with a shared Model Context Protocol server that orchestrates tasks via the Parsl workflow engine. The implementation uses the open-weight gpt-oss-120b model to run a high-throughput screening campaign over the CoRE MOF database for atmospheric water harvesting on the Aurora supercomputer.
A.research_plan: (1) The scalability and bottleneck-removal claim is supported by a demonstration on the Aurora supercomputer, using orchestration overhead and task completion as evaluation criteria. (2) The applicability claim is supported by the high-throughput screening run over the CoRE MOF database for atmospheric water harvesting. The abstract does not state baseline single-agent comparisons, ablation conditions, or explicit failure thresholds.

B.problem: Autonomous-science agents currently execute experiments as an unmanaged, sequential subroutine—reason, run one candidate, analyze, then reason again—despite mature scheduling, caching, and speculative-execution machinery available for batch compute.
B.motivation: Applying that machinery to agent experiment loops could reduce wall-clock time and idle GPU compute and make multi-hour agent loops resumable.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed distributed execution engine sits between a research agent and its pool of compute workers. It memoizes experiment results by content addressing keyed on full provenance; schedules experiments via a dependency DAG inferred from observed file-access traces; and speculatively executes likely successor experiments during model deliberation gaps, using idempotent checkpoints to make multi-hour agent loops resumable. The proposal also defines a worker-scaling evaluation protocol measuring wall-clock time to a fixed quality threshold as a function of worker count, duplication rate, and GPU idle fraction.
B.research_plan: (1) The central speedup and quality claim is tested on objective-verifier research tasks under the proposed worker-scaling protocol, measuring wall-clock time to a fixed quality threshold as a function of worker count, duplication rate, and GPU idle fraction. (2) The duplication-rate and GPU-idle-fraction axes assess reuse and scheduling/speculation behavior; support is near-linear wall-clock scaling until task-level parallelism saturates with preserved or improved final scores, while sublinear scaling, high duplication, or degraded quality would fail. (3) No retrieved research-agent benchmark currently measures this protocol, so the evaluation itself introduces the design.

A.problem: Current LLM-based scientific agents face limitations in iterative hypothesis refinement and experimental design.
A.motivation: Improving the efficiency and effectiveness of LLM-based scientific agents would promote accelerated scientific discovery across diverse domains.
A.proposed_approach: A feedback-driven multi-agent system for LLM-based scientific agents that integrates a feedback loop to support iterative hypothesis refinement and experimental design.
A.research_plan: The system will be evaluated on the BoxingGym benchmark, focusing on experimental design and model discovery; the abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, or failure conditions.

B.problem: Current autonomous scientific research systems, even those using large language models and agentic architectures, are constrained by fixed workflows and toolsets that prevent adaptation to evolving tasks and environments.
B.motivation: Adaptation to evolving tasks and environments is needed to automate a broad range of computationally accessible scientific tasks; dynamic tool discovery and experimental feedback make such adaptation tractable, and an open-source platform can support community-driven development.
B.proposed_approach: The framework automatically synthesizes task-specific multi-agent workflows and iteratively refines them through experimental feedback. A meta-orchestrator generates workflow topologies, and code-generating agents execute subtasks by invoking tools and scientific software libraries discovered through the Model Context Protocol. An LLM-based judge scores executions, and the resulting feedback drives workflow refinement. The system is released as an open-source platform with fully logged execution traces and archived workflows to support auditability.
B.research_plan: Evidence: (1) evaluation on ScienceAgentBench using DeepSeek-V3.2, with success rate compared against single-agent baselines and static multi-agent configurations; (2) analysis of heterogeneous model responses to multi-agent decomposition and iterative learning; (3) open-source release with modular, tool-agnostic design and logged execution traces/archived workflows as evidence for extensibility and auditability. No explicit failure conditions or matched-budget details are stated.

A.problem: AI systems generate scientific ideas at scale, but there is no reproducible, proxy-based mechanism to assess their soundness and feasibility before expensive experimental validation; existing approaches focus narrowly on novelty, rely on drift-prone human judgment, or validate only post-hoc via experiment.
A.motivation: A reproducible pre-experimental assessment would avoid expensive validation and make large-scale AI-generated scientific idea generation more reliably triaged and tractable.
A.proposed_approach: A domain-agnostic evaluation framework for AI-generated scientific ideas that combines automated structural soundness critique (dimensional analysis, constraint checking), literature-grounded plausibility assessment, and self-evaluation by reasoning LLMs to produce reproducible quality scores. It treats critique signals as stable proxies rather than gold-standard labels and uses a multi-signal fusion method designed to be resilient to evaluator drift.
A.research_plan: (1) The claim that the framework produces reproducible quality scores is evaluated by constructing a benchmark of 500+ scientific ideas across three domains with expert annotation and comparing the proposed quality scores to expert soundness judgments. (2) The claim of stability against human judgment drift is evaluated by checking agreement across evaluator populations and time windows. Support requires agreement with expert soundness judgments and stability across those populations and time windows; the abstract does not specify baselines, compute/parameter matching, or failure conditions beyond that agreement/stability expectation.

B.problem: It remains unclear whether large language models can judge the methodological viability of research proposals before time and computational resources are committed, because existing benchmarks rarely test this capability.
B.motivation: Autonomous research agents aim to accelerate discovery by automating the research pipeline, so a reliable early check of proposal soundness could avoid wasted time and computation.
B.proposed_approach: A curated benchmark of 1,099 machine-learning research proposals reconstructed from ICLR submissions, labeled with reviewer soundness sub-scores, and audited against source papers. The benchmark is interpreted as measuring proposal-level soundness rather than exact full-paper review outcomes. It is applied to 12 frontier large language models under standard and aggressive prompting, with controls for public-corpus contamination, paper-identifying phrases, surface features, and human audit quality.
B.research_plan: Claims are tested as follows. (1) Benchmark validity is supported by reconstruction from ICLR submissions, reviewer soundness sub-scores, and audit against source papers. (2) The judgment behavior of 12 frontier large language models is evaluated under standard and aggressive prompting. (3) Separate controls probe public-corpus contamination, paper-identifying phrases, surface features, and human audit quality; the failure condition would be if a single confounder explains the observed judgment pattern.

A.problem: LLM-based agents can automate neuroimaging workflows, but their susceptibility to hallucination limits their credibility in scientific use; current automation is not auditable scientific computation.
A.motivation: Making LLM-driven neuroimaging automation auditable would let researchers automate heterogeneous, multimodal, multistage workflows without sacrificing credibility.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework takes free-text research questions and neuroimaging datasets and converts them into executable analysis plans, validated outputs, and structured reports. Planning is disease- and tool-aware. A deterministic verification layer inspects every claim before it is retained for reporting, checking it against tool-derived evidence and domain axioms.
A.research_plan: (1) Planning capability is tested on an expert-curated benchmark of 110 neuroimaging tasks, with direct LLM queries as the comparison condition. (2) Hallucination resistance is tested through controlled injection of error classes, with detection and false positives evaluated under an explicit axiom bank and trust assumptions. (3) External validity is tested through case studies of spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, comparing outputs with established pathology and independent expert analyses.

B.problem: In autonomous AI scientist systems, agents frequently fail to execute rigorous verification procedures, leading to silent code crashes, hallucinated experimental results, and ungrounded scientific claims in generated manuscripts.
B.motivation: Because these systems already generate hypotheses, code, and manuscripts, unverified outputs can propagate false scientific claims; execution-grounded verification is needed to make such pipelines trustworthy before reporting.
B.proposed_approach: The framework operates between experiment execution and manuscript drafting. It combines dynamic execution sandboxes with runtime trace-log anomaly detection and Vision-Language Model cross-checking of figures and outputs. Verification is grounded in multi-modal validation, systematically comparing generated plots against raw data logs and known physical or statistical bounds. The system uses this to catch silent failures and prevent false scientific claims before reporting.
B.research_plan: Evaluation uses standardized AI-scientist benchmark tasks, measuring execution fidelity, hallucinated success rates, and robustness/reproducibility of scientific reports for the proposed framework relative to standard pipelines. The abstract does not name specific baselines, state matched compute, or give an explicit failure condition.

A.problem: Existing AI research assistants focus on paper writing or code generation and do not cover the full deep learning experiment lifecycle, leaving autonomous hypothesis formation, code implementation, training execution, result analysis, and iterative refinement unaddressed.
A.motivation: Around-the-clock autonomous experiment loops could accelerate deep learning research and reduce experiment cost, especially if LLM API overhead during long training runs and unbounded context growth can be controlled.
A.proposed_approach: The open-source framework uses multiple LLM agents to execute the full experiment lifecycle: forming hypotheses, implementing code, running training, analyzing results, and refining iteratively. Training-time monitoring relies only on process-level checks and log-file reads, incurring no LLM API cost while training. A memory architecture keeps context bounded at roughly 5,000 characters regardless of runtime. The leader-worker multi-agent design equips each worker with only 3–5 tools to limit per-call token overhead; code is publicly available.
A.research_plan: (1) The lifecycle claim is supported by sustained deployments over 30+ days and four concurrent projects. (2) The monitoring claim is assessed by measuring LLM API cost during training under process-level checks and log-file reads. (3) The memory and minimal-toolset claims are assessed by tracking context size over runtime and per-call token overhead in the leader-worker architecture. The abstract reports completed experiment cycles, per-24-hour cost, and baseline metric improvements but states no explicit failure conditions or matched resource settings.

B.problem: Current LLM-based systems for scientific research focus on isolated tasks and lack comprehensive end-to-end autonomous capabilities.
B.motivation: The rapid advancement of LLMs makes it timely to integrate their strengths with machine learning engineering and laboratory automation to enable more complete automation of scientific research.
B.proposed_approach: An integrated framework that uses LLMs for hypothesis generation, experimental planning, and scientific writing, combined with machine learning engineering and laboratory automation tools for experiment execution and analysis, aimed at end-to-end autonomous AI scientists.
B.research_plan: The framework will be evaluated on LAB-Bench and AutoExperiment, and its performance will be assessed in real-world scientific research scenarios; no failure condition or held-matched comparison is specified.

A.problem: Automated scientific workflows in autonomous AI scientist systems frequently suffer from unmitigated coding errors, metric misuse, data leakage, and post-hoc selection bias, which can elevate spurious findings into published claims.
A.motivation: Recent empirical audits reveal this implementation and verification bottleneck at a time when autonomous systems are already producing end-to-end research papers, making it necessary to integrate verification before spurious findings reach publication.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is an agentic verification layer interposed between experiment execution and manuscript generation. It automatically extracts domain-specific behavioral invariants from the generated research hypothesis, such as monotonicity under noise, permutation invariance, and sanity checks against random baselines. It then synthesizes property-based test suites from these invariants and actively stress-tests the experimental implementation before any scientific writing begins.
A.research_plan: The evaluation is a comprehensive design across standard machine learning benchmarking domains, applying the proposed verification layer to automated scientific workflows before manuscript generation. The intended evidence is whether the framework catches hallucinated improvements and silent pipeline bugs. The abstract does not specify named baselines, metrics, ablations, or explicit failure conditions.

B.problem: The academic integrity of autonomous AI scientist systems has not been systematically evaluated, particularly when task completion conflicts with honest acknowledgment of infeasibility.
B.motivation: Such systems are increasingly deployed for autonomous research, making integrity failures costly and a dilemmatic evaluation paradigm necessary to reveal trained dispositions rather than task capability.
B.proposed_approach: The work constructs a benchmark of 33 scenarios across 11 trap categories, each designed so that honest acknowledgment of failure is the only correct response while task completion requires misconduct. It evaluates seven state-of-the-art LLMs over 231 runs. A prompt ablation study manipulates explicit completion pressure to separate its role from underlying synthetic-data generation behavior. The benchmark is publicly released.
B.research_plan: (1) Benchmark evaluation across 231 runs and seven state-of-the-art LLMs measures integrity violations and disclosure patterns in dilemmatic and missing-data scenarios, bearing on the first two claims. (2) Prompt ablation removes explicit completion pressure and compares undisclosed fabrication and synthesis-rate metrics; support for the third claim requires undisclosed fabrication to fall while synthesis rate remains unchanged, whereas a parallel fall in both would indicate only a prompt-level effect. The abstract does not state matched compute or parameter settings across models beyond using the same benchmark scenarios.

A.problem: LLM-based research agents have advanced through agent orchestration but largely overlook scientific knowledge orchestration; existing works reduce papers to abstracts, surface mentions, and flat citation edges, omitting key entities, claims, evidence, mechanisms, and method lineages needed for scientific reasoning.
A.motivation: Scientific reasoning and multi-hop research over papers require richer, machine-usable scientific knowledge that captures full-paper structure and content, not just abstracts and citation edges.
A.proposed_approach: An end-to-end knowledge orchestration pipeline converts raw documents into agent-native scientific knowledge graphs under a unifying theoretical foundation. It comprises a multimodal parser whose five-module schema captures entities, multimodal evidence, citations, and typed inter-entity relations across the full paper rather than abstracts alone; a 4B information-extraction backbone trained with GRPO under a rule-based reward; and a tri-source agent interface that unifies web search, multimodal graph retrieval, and cross-document traversal. The pipeline is applied to 2.46 million scientific papers across six subjects to build a large knowledge graph, with a one-million-paper subset released and the full graph accessible via a provided link; it is also described as extendable to general-domain corpora and schema-conformant data synthesis.
A.research_plan: The paper reports extensive experiments across scientific information extraction, knowledge graph construction, and multi-hop scientific reasoning. The abstract states these experiments demonstrate superiority but does not specify baselines, metrics, ablations, or failure conditions.

B.problem: Autoresearch systems such as AI-Researcher and Jr. AI Scientist now execute the full scientific workflow, yet every existing evaluation of them is end-to-end or static, and every existing failure-attribution method targets generic multi-agent orchestration rather than the stage structure of a research pipeline.
B.motivation: This gap matters because AI-scientist systems now run the full workflow; diagnosing the true failing stage enables cheaper, targeted repair instead of full-pipeline retry.
B.proposed_approach: The framework models an AI-scientist pipeline as a staged causal graph with stages for hypothesis specification, experimental design, implementation/execution, and analysis/claim verification, each emitting checkable artifacts such as a falsifiable hypothesis, a metric/split protocol, executable minimal code with per-function unit tests, and recomputed results. It contributes a stage-annotated fault-injection benchmark built from re-implementation tasks with gold code and tests in the style of Scientist-Bench, MLRC-Bench, and Gravity-Bench, executed by at least three open AI-scientist systems, with failing traces labeled by the true failing stage and minimal per-stage repair patches. It also contributes an interventional attribution protocol that re-executes each failing run under counterfactual stage neutralization and gold-patch replay, scoring each stage by the delta it produces in the final objective metric, and an attribution-conditioned repair loop that patches only the attributed stage.
B.research_plan: For the stage-localization claim, the framework compares stage-localization accuracy of the stage-grounded attribution against the best log-level LLM judge on the stage-annotated fault-injection benchmark. For the counterfactual replay claim, it re-executes failing runs under counterfactual stage neutralization and gold-patch replay and checks whether the injected stage is top-1 cause in single-fault cases. For the targeted repair claim, it runs the attribution-conditioned repair loop and measures recovered final-metric performance and iteration cost relative to full-pipeline retry. The benchmark is built from re-implementation tasks with gold code and tests and is executed by at least three open AI-scientist systems; a negative result on the targeted-repair claim is treated as publishable evidence about the implementation gap.

A.problem: Autonomous AI scientists for scientific computing often propose mathematically unstable or physically inconsistent PDEs and scientific laws due to hallucinations or unconstrained symbolic regression searches, causing wasted execution cycles and divergent numerical simulations.
A.motivation: Verification and physical consistency checking before full-scale training would avoid wasted computation and divergent simulations in autonomous scientific discovery for continuum mechanics and dynamical systems.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed layer intercepts agent-generated code and symbolic equations before full-scale training. It routes them through a lightweight differentiable numerical sandbox and an invariant-preserving data store that enforces conservation laws, boundedness, and physical symmetry constraints. It computes real-time stability metrics and physical consistency scores and feeds precise negative feedback and structured state management back to the agent.
A.research_plan: Evidence consists of extensive evaluation scenarios across chaotic and noisy PDEs. The abstract names no specific baselines, metrics, or ablations, and states no explicit failure condition or held-matched factors; the efficiency, redundancy, and physical-law adherence claims are supported by these scenarios.

B.problem: Current data-driven discovery of physical laws is split: Hamiltonian neural networks lack interpretability and enforce strict structural assumptions, while standard symbolic regression suffers algebraic explosions in high-dimensional phase spaces and does not incorporate deep physical invariants such as Noether-derived conservation laws.
B.motivation: Unifying neural and symbolic discovery could yield compact, physically interpretable Hamiltonians and conserved quantities, and autonomous LLM agents provide a mechanism to coordinate these previously separate components.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is an autonomous LLM-agent system that co-optimizes neural Hamiltonian representations and symbolic expressions. It runs an iterative agentic loop that coordinates natural-language hypothesis generation, automatic Lie symmetry detection, and reward-guided symbolic regression. The agent proposes coordinate transformations and symmetry-adapted functional ansatzes, evaluates them against symplectic consistency and conservation laws, and iteratively refines the models.
B.research_plan: The evidence is experimental on classical and relativistic multi-body dynamics, testing whether the approach discovers compact, physically interpretable Hamiltonians and conserved quantities under noisy, partial observations. The abstract gives no named baselines or explicit quantitative failure conditions.

A.problem: Existing AI methods, especially large language models, support individual tasks like hypothesis generation and experimental design but do not reproduce the collaborative, team-based way in which diverse experts jointly address complex scientific problems.
A.motivation: Accelerating scientific discovery requires tools that can emulate collaborative expert teamwork, not only individual reasoning.
A.proposed_approach: An enhanced LLM-based multi-agent system that gives the agents a time-varying knowledge exchange mechanism and a review process with two separate diversity criteria; it is intended to emulate collaborative scientific teamwork for idea generation.
A.research_plan: The paper reports comprehensive experiments comparing the proposed system with state-of-the-art methods, using novelty of generated scientific ideas as the evaluation target.

B.problem: Many existing AI scientist systems rely on rigid interaction protocols and coarse-grained novelty tests, which impede long-term creative exploration in autonomous scientific ideation.
B.motivation: Massive language models show promise for autonomous scientific ideation, so more flexible multi-agent collaboration and finer-grained novelty assessment may unlock long-term creative exploration.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework organizes multiple agents into rotating conversation groups using a World Café-style collaborative structure. A multi-strategy turn-taking scheduler distributes speaking turns adaptively based on relevance, participation balance, and self-reported willingness. Novelty assessment incorporates a finer-grained idea novelty metric for more detailed evaluation.
B.research_plan: Evaluation compares the framework against single-agent and multi-agent baselines using a total novelty measure, under regulated discussion cost conditions and using public academic knowledge graphs. The design also includes component-level assessment of the turn-taking scheduler and the novelty metric's effect on creative performance. No explicit failure condition or matched compute/parameter controls are stated.

A.problem: Experiment selection in end-to-end AI scientist systems is rarely posed as an explicit epistemic decision: the next measurement is whatever falls out of writing and executing code that tests the hypothesis, rather than a measurement chosen to separate the focal hypothesis from a concrete rival. Classical adaptive design optimization addresses this when the rival set is known, but no retrieved system closes the loop from natural-language hypotheses to executable rival models to an information-optimal choice.
A.motivation: An explicit code-based discriminator could allocate scarce experiments to distinguish hypotheses under a query budget, improving discovery efficiency; recent LLM scientist pipelines make natural-language hypotheses available but lack the adaptive selection loop that would realize this.
A.proposed_approach: The work proposes a benchmark of 12 generative scientific environments in which hidden ground truth is drawn from a terrain of confusable functional classes and an agent must identify the true class under a query budget. A planner materializes the agent's articulated rivals as executable code, maintains a Bayesian posterior over models, scores candidate experiments by model-discrimination expected information gain, and either recommends the next measurement or serves as a reference against which the agent's own choices are measured.
A.research_plan: The benchmark's hidden ground-truth classes and query-budget settings are the evidence intended to support claim (1) that experiment decisiveness is quantified. For claim (2), the work compares confirmatory LLM-selected experiments with utility-optimal choices in the same environments, and measures whether the proposed code-based discriminator's choices reduce that gap; the central claim fails if no systematic gap appears or if the discriminator does not close most of it.

B.problem: Autonomous research systems are predominantly evaluated and built as experimenter-defined objective optimizers, measuring how few trials are needed to maximize a yield or property, but most scientific questions ask which mechanism generated the data, a causal question that can only be answered by experiments that discriminate between rival explanations.
B.motivation: Making mechanistic disambiguation measurable would convert the recurring critique that optimizing is not discovering into a benchmarked quantity, enabling development of systems that economically resolve which mechanism is true rather than which condition scores best.
B.proposed_approach: A benchmark-and-agent suite for closed-loop mechanistic disambiguation is built around a pool of rival rate-law mechanisms represented as structured ODE families with parametric uncertainty and noise in a flow-/droplet-chemistry-inspired emulator. Agents must select parallel batches of experiments that separate the plausible mechanisms at minimum cost. Six controller classes are compared: an explicit-posterior information-theoretic discrimination controller, objective-reward Bayesian optimization, LLM planners with and without code tools, a falsification-style agent, and random design. The suite comprises 20 tasks with controlled initial ambiguity, pool completeness, budget, and noise, and trace-logging evaluation estimates posterior calibration and false certainty.
B.research_plan: (1) The central claim is tested by running the six controllers on the 20-task suite and comparing experimental cost to identify the true mechanism and extrapolation on probes designed to reveal mechanistic disagreement; support requires strictly lower cost and better extrapolation for the expected-information-gain controller than objective-optimizing or LLM-only controllers, and failure is the absence of such advantage. (2) The benchmark's adequacy is assessed through controlled initial ambiguity, pool completeness, budget, and noise, and through trace-logging estimates of posterior calibration and false certainty. The abstract does not state any compute or parameter matching across controllers.
